Senior engineers coached junior colleagues; peer-led demos, live-project learning, and career-development conversations supported skill growth. Performance feedback came from recent pairing partners, product managers, and team anchors—not simply visibility to the boss. answer_md:
🐾 At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, team autonomy didn’t work consistently just because Matt had designed the organization that way.

The center was flat from day one, with autonomy at the team level, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. But many practitioners came from legacy delivery organizations where top-down, command-and-control patterns were the norm. Those habits reasserted themselves: decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. Matt describes converting people to the model as requiring “enforcement and revalidation, multiple times,” and says “the path was bumpy.”

Psychological safety also wasn’t uniform. As the centers scaled to **150+** practitioners, isolated pockets of fear of blame persisted. Some team members still hesitated to share ideas or take risks, limiting innovation and engagement in those areas.

Matt responded by reinforcing shared decision-making authority across product managers, designers, and engineers. Anchors and team leads focused on removing obstacles rather than controlling outcomes. He established clear, flexible decision-making guidelines tied to project objectives and used continuous retrospectives to revisit how teams were working. He also held open, growth-focused feedback conversations, shared his own experiences with mistakes, and organized non-punitive post-mortems and low-stakes experiments.

The stories report fewer decision bottlenecks, improved morale and engagement, and reduced turnover afterward. They do not quantify those changes or document a permanent failure. The specific shortfall was that the flat structure and stated culture did not, on their own, stop teams from reverting to waiting for permission.

answer_md:
🐾 At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt’s initial working model did not prevent a quality crisis.

In early **2020**, he launched the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement to modernize the Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. He brought in a balanced team and emphasized test-driven development. A couple of months in, as the pandemic moved everyone to remote work, the client reported rising defects—even though the dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt found that an engineer was building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story and writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete, but defects went undetected. The backlog was also part of the failure: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories, brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the team, and had the code and test cases redone. Coaching became hands-on: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing through “I do, we do, you do.”

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Defect rates dropped, and client confidence was restored through transparency and visible improvement. The story does not report a numerical defect reduction. Matt’s stated lesson was that test-coverage metrics mean nothing without the practice behind them, and cultural transformation requires consistent coaching—not just process change.

answer_md:
🐾 At **Norfolk Southern**, the balanced-team approach initially failed to prevent a quality crisis.

In early **2020**, Matt launched the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement to modernize the client’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. The team emphasized test-driven development within a Lean Startup approach. A couple of months in, as the pandemic forced work remote, the client reported rising defects—even though dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt found that an engineer was building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story and writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete, but defects went undetected. The backlog also lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done. The balanced team and stated engineering practices had not ensured that the actual work followed those practices.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly, including the backlog problems. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work alongside the team and redo the code and tests. Coaching included boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and “I do, we do, you do” pairing.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. The story reports restored client confidence, but no numerical defect reduction. Matt’s stated lesson was that metrics mean nothing without the practice behind them, and cultural transformation requires consistent coaching—not just process change.

🐾 Matt’s payments work includes building corporate payment engines and gateways, migrating legacy payment systems, and simplifying virtual-payment API integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed capabilities beyond Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform. Regional systems had different data models, payment formats, entitlement structures, and compliance requirements. Matt led a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He also designed the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**, coordinating with Bottomline on where native connectivity ended and bank-specific engineering was required.

For migration, Matt worked with compliance teams to verify legacy data, preserve regulatory traceability, and consolidate client configurations, entitlements, and transaction histories without disruption to live payments. He owned production incident response, cross-team root-cause analysis, status updates, and daily leadership calls. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**; the gateway gave treasurers a single entry point across regional payment systems.

At **American Express**, Virtual Payments Platform adoption was slowed by missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, no sandbox, and testing dependencies. Matt partnered with business and technical teams through North Star and Discovery and Framing workshops. His work included Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, a secure sandbox, virtualized testing environments, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time decreased, and the portal team exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261 story points**.

🐾 Matt describes his leadership approach as “listen first, align around purpose, and move intentionally.” His stated philosophy is to lead with empathy, clarity, and purpose, with a “permit to fail” learning environment and balanced teams: Product + Engineering + Design together.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, building an organization meant creating ways to hire, evaluate, develop, and promote people without adding layers of managers. Matt grew the organization from a **10-person** pilot to **150+ practitioners**, with **11–13** practice and client leads reporting directly to him. Teams held execution power through autonomy, collective code ownership, and fluid role rotation.

He paired senior engineers with junior colleagues, embedded learning in live client projects, and established weekly tech talks with peer-led demos. New joiners received a month of enablement followed by round-robin pairing with seasoned practitioners. Practice leads reserved Friday afternoons for career-development conversations. The organization recorded near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**, and multiple hires were promoted.

For performance evaluation, Matt used evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and team anchors rather than a manager’s impressions. He ran monthly feedback sessions, made expectations explicit by career level, and owned final hiring decisions, compensation allocation, and decisions to end performance remediation.

He also held delivery and financial accountability. At **Fiserv**, he helped recover an **\$8.5M** program the client was ready to cancel: it finished **3% under budget**, preserving **\$255K**, avoiding **\$500K** in contractual penalties, and securing a **\$3M** extension. At the centers, he required internal bench deployment before external contractor spending—even when that decision was escalated.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center.

The center was designed flat from day one: team-level autonomy, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. But many practitioners came from legacy delivery organizations where top-down, command-and-control patterns were the norm. Those habits returned: decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. Getting people to work differently took enforcement and revalidation, multiple times; the path was bumpy.

Matt established cross-functional teams of product managers, designers, and engineers with shared ownership and decision-making authority. Instead of making team leads the approval point, he had anchors and leads focus on removing obstacles rather than controlling outcomes. 🐾 Here’s how Matt describes—and practiced—his leadership.

Matt’s stated philosophy is to lead with empathy, clarity, and purpose: “listen first, align around purpose, and move intentionally.” He describes a “permit to fail” learning environment and balanced teams with Product, Engineering, and Design together. Across his work, that included Execution & Delivery, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Talent & Enablement.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, the challenge was running a **150+**-practitioner organization without managers sitting on daily teams or adding middle-management layers. Matt kept a deliberately flat structure through **11–13** practice and client leads. Teams held execution power, with collective code ownership, fluid role rotation, and experienced engineering anchors working alongside product managers and designers.

He built feedback around the people doing the work together—not visibility to the boss. Practice leads gathered evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors. Matt ran monthly feedback capture sessions, with each individual’s People Lead present to relay actionable feedback. He also made expectations explicit through role and responsibility matrices and owned final hiring decisions, compensation allocation, and end-of-remediation calls.

When cloud-native knowledge gaps slowed delivery, he paired senior engineers with junior teammates, embedded learning in live client projects, and introduced weekly peer-led demos and engineering practice forums. Career development conversations had reserved time rather than being left to chance. His NEW IT SKILLS NOW curriculum trained **300+ professionals**.

The CIC grew from a **10-person** pilot to **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**. During scaling pushes, its hiring process added **4–**6 practitioners** per week**, while limiting interview demands so delivery continued.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time decreased, and the portal team exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261** story points.

🐾 Here’s how Matt describes it: “listen first, align around purpose, and move intentionally.” His leadership work spans Talent & Enablement, Org & Working-Model Transformation, and Execution & Delivery.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, cloud-native technologies were evolving faster than teams could keep up. The organization grew from a **10-person** pilot to **150+** practitioners, with **11–13** direct-report leads and near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**. The hiring process used hands-on TDD pairing auditions rather than relying only on interviews, sustaining **4–6** net-new practitioners per week during scaling pushes while limiting each practitioner’s interview load to protect delivery time.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center.

The center was designed to be flat, with autonomy at the team level and collective ownership. But many practitioners arrived from legacy delivery organizations where top-down, command-and-control patterns were the norm. Those habits reasserted themselves: decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. Establishing the model was not the same as getting people to live it; Matt had to enforce and revalidate it multiple times.

He encouraged people to challenge assumptions without fear of judgment.

Teams reported higher engagement and satisfaction. Decentralized decisions removed bottlenecks, and teams consistently met project milestones. Where fear of blame had persisted, morale improved and turnover declined. Matt is a builder; in this example, the work included changing who made decisions and making it safer for people to speak honestly.

🐾 Found it! Matt’s payments work includes corporate payment engines, global gateway integration, legacy migration, and developer onboarding.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed more than an out-of-box deployment of Bottomline’s WebSeries platform. Regional systems had different data models and entitlement structures, while payment types had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements. Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across **Accenture** and the bank, defining where native platform capabilities ended and bespoke engineering was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules, including NACHA file validation, Message Authentication Code security, and payment-type-specific permissions. He built sanctions screening and risk-based approval controls into payment flows. For the gateway, he mapped local payment rules into message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**, rather than retaining fragmented point-to-point integrations. He also led payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability without disruption to live payment operations. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,**000+ client**s** across **180+ countries**.

At **American Express**, the Virtual Payments Platform offered flexible APIs, but missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, and no sandbox hindered adoption. Matt’s work addressed integration itself—not just the portal interface. He developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, sample integrations, use case-driven documentation, and a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. Environment virtualization reduced downstream dependencies and enabled earlier testing; CI/CD kept documentation and APIs synchronized with backend changes.

He used Lean Product and XP practices and a Client Onboarding Test Drive to gather user feedback. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time decreased, and the portal team delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond its delivery commitment.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center.

The center was designed to be flat: autonomy at the team level, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. As the center scaled to **150+ practitioners**, pockets of fear of blame also emerged. Matt regularly spoke with team members about their challenges and aspirations, held open retrospectives, and shared his own experiences with risk-taking and mistakes. Team members were encouraged to challenge assumptions and share ideas without fear of judgment.

Decentralized decision-making removed bottlenecks. Teams reported higher engagement and satisfaction, and consistently met project milestones. The work addressing fear of blame improved morale, increased innovative solutions, and reduced turnover. Matt describes himself as a builder; here, the work included changing who made decisions and how teams raised concerns—not just establishing an organization chart.

🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work across corporate banking, virtual payments, and card processing.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed payment capabilities beyond Bottomline’s out-of-box WebSeries platform. Regional connectivity also differed across **12 countries**. Matt managed a blended team of **40+** and defined where platform configuration ended and bespoke engineering was required. He delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules, alongside payment-type-specific entitlements, Message Authentication Code security, sanctions screening, and risk-based approval controls. He also designed the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing into clearing networks and internal compliance and settlement systems. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+** clients across **180+ countries**; the gateway unified payment connectivity across **12 countries**.

At **American Express**, Virtual Payments Platform adoption lagged because clients lacked SDKs, usable documentation, and a sandbox. Matt co-created a developer portal with Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, sample integrations, “day-one” guides, and use case-driven API documentation. Rather than leaving developers dependent on downstream systems for testing, he introduced environment virtualization and a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. Discovery and Framing workshops, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive guided the portal redesign. API trial usage increased within **3 months**, onboarding time declined, and the team delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond its commitment.

At **Fiserv**, a white-label card portal faced missed deadlines, poor quality, and threatened cancellation. Matt reset the backlog and timelines, coordinated **3 external vendors**, and managed the integration layer connecting legacy mainframe payment processing to a Java EE/Spring portal. Delivery stabilized within **3 months**. The **\$8.5M** program finished **3% under budget**, met all **47 acceptance criteria**, and launched with **zero critical defects**. The portal processed **\$45M** in transactions in its first month with **99.**97%** uptime**.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed payment capabilities beyond Bottomline Technologies’ out-of-box platform. It served **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+ countries**, with distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and workflow requirements. Matt managed a **40+**-person blended team across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax payment modules, plus Message Authentication Code security, payment-type-specific entitlements, sanctions screening, and real-time global reporting. He also delivered the centralized gateway handling message transformation, protocol translation, and payment routing across **12 countries**. ACCESS and the gateway launched in **April 2011**; Matt owned production incident response across releases and migrations.

At **Fiserv**, the **\$8.5M** white-label card portal had missed multiple deadlines, and contract cancellation was on the table. The platform served **2M+ cardholders** across **15 financial institutions**. Matt coordinated **45 team members** and **3 external vendors**, managing the integration layer connecting legacy mainframe payment processing to a Java EE/Spring portal through MuleSoft, Tibco, and WebMethods. He stabilized delivery within **3 months**. The program finished **3% under budget**, met all **47 acceptance criteria**, and launched with **zero critical defects**. The portal processed **\$45M** in transactions in its first month with **99.**97%** uptime**.

At **American Express**, Virtual Payments Platform adoption lagged because SDKs were missing, documentation was fragmented, and clients had no sandbox. Matt co-created the developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and built a secure sandbox. He also introduced virtualized testing environments, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch; the team delivered over **261 additional story points** beyond its commitment.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Centers, cloud-native technologies were evolving faster than teams could keep up. Meanwhile, a deliberately flat organization meant managers weren’t sitting beside practitioners on their daily teams. Matt built coaching and feedback into the work rather than relying on a supervisor’s observations. Senior engineers paired with junior colleagues, teams held weekly peer-led demos, and new joiners rotated through pairing with seasoned practitioners. Career development conversations had reserved time on Friday afternoons.

He ran the **150+**-person organization through **11–13** practice and client leads, with balanced teams holding execution power, collective code ownership, and fluid role rotation. For performance reviews, leads gathered evidence from recent pair partners, product managers, and team anchors. Advancement rested on that peer evidence—not visibility to the boss. Matt made every final hiring decision and owned compensation allocation and end-of-remediation calls. The organization recorded near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**.

With **Fortune **500 Client**s**, the problem was often unchanged silos and handoffs beneath newly modernized technology. Matt coached teams using “I do, we do, you do” and ran **6-week** Agility Coaching Labs on their actual work. Teams adopted product-centric practices and reduced costs **15–35%**.

He also held financial boundaries. In one fixed-fee engagement, he rejected a request for **2** external contractors and required cross-skilling and redeployment of **2** internal practitioners instead. The decision was escalated, and it stood.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center.

The center was designed flat from day one, with autonomy at the team level and collective ownership. But many practitioners arrived from legacy delivery organizations where top-down, command-and-control patterns were normal. Those habits returned: decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. Establishing the model wasn’t enough—Matt had to enforce and revalidate it repeatedly, and the path was bumpy.

Matt brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in cross-functional teams with shared ownership and decision-making authority. Rather than having leaders control outcomes, he made their role facilitation: anchors and team leads focused on removing obstacles while teams owned decisions. He established clear, flexible guidelines so teams could make decisions within project objectives instead of waiting for permission.

He also embedded continuous retrospectives, iterative development, and user-centered design so teams could adjust based on feedback and user needs. Where fear of blame persisted as the center scaled to **150+** practitioners, Matt spoke with team members about their challenges and aspirations, held open retrospectives focused on growth-oriented feedback, and shared his own experiences with mistakes and risk-taking.

Teams reported higher engagement and satisfaction. Decentralized decisions removed bottlenecks, and teams consistently met project milestones. Matt describes himself as a “builder”; here, the work included changing who made decisions and how people could challenge assumptions—not just establishing an organization chart.

🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work, from payment engines to developer onboarding.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, ACCESS Next Generation needed more than Bottomline Technologies’ out-of-box platform. Regional systems had different data models, payment formats, entitlement structures, and compliance requirements. The global portal served **135,000+** corporate, financial institution, government, and municipal clients across **180+ countries**; its payments gateway connected payment operations across **12 countries**.

Matt was Technology Delivery Lead, managing a **40+** blended team across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He designed and delivered bespoke ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. That included NACHA file validation, foreign-exchange integration, payment-type-specific permissions, and Message Authentication Code security so users could verify payment integrity before release. He also built integrations for transaction monitoring, risk-based approval controls, and sanctions screening.

For the gateway, Matt designed message transformation, protocol translation, and routing between payment rails and internal compliance, settlement, and reporting systems. He led payments-workstream data migration, preserving client configurations, entitlements, transaction histories, and compliance traceability. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; migration completed without disruption to live payment operations. Matt also owned on-call and critical production incident response.

At **American Express**, the challenge was adoption of its Virtual Payments Platform: missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, no sandbox, and downstream dependencies were slowing integration. Matt led developer-experience work spanning a modern portal, Java/.NET/Python SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, and secure virtualized testing environments. His team used Lean Product and XP practices and validated onboarding through a Client Onboarding Test Drive.

API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, and client onboarding time decreased. The portal modernization team exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261 story points** of customer-focused value.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built the organization.

The growth wasn’t a single team expanding from **4** engineers to **150+**. Matt’s earlier delivery scope included a **3–5-person** interface team at **AT&T**; the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers at **Accenture** grew from a **10-person** pilot to **150+ practitioners** across engineering, product, and design. Many new hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience, while client demand required teams that could deliver—not just complete training.

Matt built a hiring engine across **4** channels: internal bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and approved job requisitions. Engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions rather than relying only on interviews. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process added **4–**6 practitioners** per week**, with interview participation capped at **2** slots per practitioner per week so recruiting did not consume delivery time or burn out interviewers.

New joiners received structured enablement and round-robin pairing with seasoned practitioners. The learning model was “I do, we do, you do,” moving people from guided work to independent delivery. Matt embedded pair programming, TDD, CI/CD, user research, and Build-Measure-Learn cycles into balanced teams—not separate training exercises.

He kept the organization deliberately flat, with **11–13** practice and client leads reporting directly to him. Weekly allocation reviews matched people to engagements and learning tracks. Experienced team anchors communicated technical progress and team needs without adding middle-management layers. Because managers weren’t sitting beside practitioners daily, evaluations drew on recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors. Career-development conversations, explicit role expectations, and promotion calibration supplied the development machinery.

The centers reached **150+ practitioners** over about **4 years**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years** and multiple hires promoted. Their **10-person** balanced teams delivered output equivalent to traditional **20-person** teams, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments.
